records.our_prose: Sometimes fruit that looks ripe on the outside is dry and pithy inside. This usually happens to fruit left on the tree too long in a hot, dry climate, especially in the desert late in the season. Heat, dryness, and over-ripeness are the causes, and the skin can look fine even when the inside has dried out.

records.our_prose: This tiny brown insect has a distinctive resting posture: it perches on new leaves at an angle, with its rear end raised and pointed upward, which is your identification clue. The young ones produce little waxy white threads and cause the new leaf tips to curl. The real danger is not the feeding itself but a fatal disease the psyllid spreads, citrus greening, so it is worth acting on even where the pest is uncommon.

records.source_context: While Asian citrus psyllid adults can feed on mature, hardened citrus leaves, all stages of this pest prefer to feed on, and therefore damage, new leaf growth . The salivary toxin that Asian citrus psyllid injects while feeding can cause the new leaf tips to turn back . Beyond feeding damage, Asian citrus psyllid vectors the lethal bacterium (Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus) that causes huanglongbing (HLB or citrus greening) disease.

records.our_prose: The defining storage feature of navels is the long on-tree hold. Late-maturing selections such as Lane Late extend the harvest and storage season the furthest, holding sound fruit into spring. The exception is hot, dry climates, where fruit left on the tree too long can granulate and dry inside, so in the desert harvest within the prime window rather than relying on the full hold. Handle fruit gently, since rind damage shortens storage life.

records.our_prose: All navel oranges are clonal bud sports or mutations tracing back to the original Washington navel, which was introduced to the United States from Bahia, Brazil in the 1870s. Variety differences are primarily in maturity timing, rind color development, and flesh pigmentation rather than tree habit or hardiness. All are seedless and parthenocarpic. In regions with marginal heat, early-coloring selections like Fukumoto may reach acceptable sugar levels sooner. Late selections like Lane Late extend the harvest window without requiring a second tree.
